title: Silicon bond model, electrons and holes

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
Silicon has four valence electrons and sits in a diamond lattice where every atom shares one covalent bond with each of four neighbours. At absolute zero every bond is complete and there are no free carriers: silicon is an insulator.

At room temperature, thermal energy occasionally breaks a bond. The freed **electron** can wander and conduct. The empty bond it leaves behind, the **hole**, can also move: a neighbouring bonded electron hops in, so the vacancy shifts. A hole behaves like a positive carrier with charge \(+q\). In the band picture, breaking a bond means lifting an electron across the bandgap \(E_g \approx 1.1\ \mathrm{eV}\) from the valence band to the conduction band.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Each broken bond makes one electron and one hole, so in pure silicon
\[ n = p = n_i \]
Atom density of silicon: about \(5\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\).
Bandgap: \(E_g = E_c - E_v \approx 1.12\ \mathrm{eV}\) at 300 K.
Conductivity counts both carriers:
\[ \sigma = q\,(n\mu_n + p\mu_p) \]

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
How rare are broken bonds? At room temperature, \(n_i \approx 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). Silicon has four bonds per atom, each shared by two atoms, which works out to about \(10^{23}\) bonds per cm³.
\[ \frac{10^{10}}{10^{23}} = 10^{-13} \]
Only about one bond in ten trillion is broken, which is why pure silicon is such a poor conductor.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Picturing a hole as a positron or a real particle. It is a missing electron in a bond.
- Thinking holes move as fast as electrons. In silicon \(\mu_p\) is roughly a third of \(\mu_n\).
- Forgetting that both carriers add to the current even though they move in opposite directions.
- Confusing the valence band (bonded electrons) with the conduction band (free electrons).

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Electrons and holes are the two carriers in every device that follows. The next steps quantify how many there are (intrinsic concentration), how doping changes the balance, and how they move (drift and diffusion).
